docket_movements.action: Opened its San Antonio robotaxi service to anyone who downloads the Waymo app, with trips to and from San Antonio International Airport included.
docket_movements.object: Robotaxi rides in San Antonio, including the airport
docket_movements.next_step: The record names no later date. Waymo's February post said the broad opening was planned for later in 2026. The docket's own key_dates entry is the October 14th effective date.
docket_movements.who_can_act: Waymo LLC sets its service rules. Riders can download the app. No public comment window is open, per the record.

docket_movements.action: Filed campaign 26E026000 for certain 5th and 6th generation automated driving systems. Defect: the software may let a vehicle slow and then drive into standing water on higher speed roadways.
docket_movements.county: Bexar for the April incidents. The recall covers the fleet nationally.
docket_movements.next_step: Remedy is listed as under development. A search summary says NHTSA's May 11th acknowledgment letter asked for a remedy description (unverified, the PDF is unread). Report date conflicts: NHTSA JSON and aggregators say May 1st, a search summary says a Part 573 submission dated May 6th. Use May 2026 until the PDF is read.
docket_movements.who_can_act: Waymo LLC (remedy and any amended Part 573 filing). NHTSA (oversight and follow-up). Public can read the federal recall record.

docket_movements.action: Modified operations to increase weather-related constraints and updated vehicle maps. NHTSA says all affected vehicles received the interim update by April 20th, 2026.
docket_movements.next_step: Permanent remedy under development. No source dated after May 2026 confirms the interim measure is still active.
docket_movements.who_can_act: Waymo LLC. NHTSA on the Part 573 remedy.

docket_movements.action: Was swept up in flood waters and washed into Salado Creek during heavy rains, per Texas Public Radio. No one was injured.
Began airport service at San Antonio International Airport for invited riders. Drop-off curbside at the terminals, pickup in the airport's designated rideshare area (TechCrunch, as of that date).
docket_movements.next_step: Airport trips opened to all app users on October 14th per Waymo.
docket_movements.who_can_act: Waymo LLC. The airport operates the pickup area.

docket_movements.action: San Antonio service was paused after the April 20th incident. TPR calls it the company's longest San Antonio pause to date and says service was expected to resume that week.
docket_movements.next_step: Resumption was expected the week of May 10th. Secondary sources date the actual restart to September 17th, 2026, so it ran months later.

docket_movements.action: EVwire (May 22nd) reports pauses in Atlanta, San Antonio, Dallas and Houston over severe weather challenges. Its dates conflict: it says the pauses began Thursday May 21st and also that San Antonio had been paused since late April. Spectrum (June 5th) reports a recent pause in Houston, Austin, Dallas and San Antonio over oncoming traffic and emergency vehicle reports. The two accounts give different reasons. Neither is confirmed by a primary source.
docket_movements.next_step: Unresolved. Do not present as settled.
docket_movements.who_can_act: Waymo LLC. TxDMV, if a state authorization question is raised.

docket_movements.action: Resumed San Antonio rides for riders who already had access, in a limited area that includes the airport (Axios, via search summary; body unread). A guide dated September 27th, 2026 says the same date and lists the service area as 60 square miles as of that date (secondary).
docket_movements.next_step: New users planned for later in 2026 (Axios, via summary). The October 14th post then opened the service to anyone with the app.

docket_movements.action: Authorization to operate automated motor vehicles commercially became enforceable under Senate Bill 2807 (89th Legislature). The authorization must be held by the commercial operator. TxDMV can suspend, revoke, cancel or restrict it after finding unsafe operation endangering the public. The public can submit concerns to the TxDMV Enforcement Division.
docket_movements.object: Commercial automated motor vehicle operators in Texas
docket_movements.next_step: The TxDMV page lists no authorized companies and does not name Waymo. Waymo's authorization status is NOT found in any source.
docket_movements.who_can_act: TxDMV, which can suspend, revoke, cancel or restrict. The public, which can submit concerns to the TxDMV Enforcement Division (the page limits these to concerns about possible serious bodily injury or death).

filmability.recommended_angle: Evidence-led news report. The record changed on a dated day (October 14th, 2026: anyone with the app, airport included), and the federal record still lists the flood fix as under development. One disclosed illustration explains the recall's mechanism. No footage exists in any fetched source.
filmability.format_and_medium: News report, evidence-led ordering. Primary approach: evidence-led imagery (the recall text, the Waymo post, the NHTSA count). Secondary approach: explanatory animation, used only for the recall's three-part sentence. Reject observed documentary (no footage) and cinematic scene (see rejected_alternatives).
filmability.viewer_question: Anyone in San Antonio can now hail a Waymo, the airport included. The federal recall covering its flood behavior still lists the permanent fix as under development. What does the record say protects a rider when the road floods?
filmability.visible_answer: The company says it tightened weather constraints and updated maps by April 20th, 2026. NHTSA lists the permanent remedy as under development. No source found describes what the weather constraint is or whether it is active now. The company's own post on the October 14th opening does not mention flooding.
filmability.opening_action: Illustrated higher-speed lane with standing water across it. A robotaxi outline appears and a label reads 'detected flooded road' (wording to be verified from TPR May 13). The outline continues into the water at reduced speed. No speed value, no depth value and no crash are drawn. A disclosed illustration caption reads: 'Illustration based on the recall wording. Not footage of the April event.' A date card follows: 'October 14th, 2026: anyone with the app.'
filmability.mechanism: Three labelled states, drawn from the recall sentence and nothing more: (1) the vehicle detects the flooded road, (2) it continues on its path, (3) it proceeds into standing water at reduced speed. Caption carries the NHTSA sentence verbatim: 'The software may allow the vehicle to slow and then drive into standing water on higher speed roadways.' Do NOT draw a stop state. No source says what the car should do instead, and drawing a correct path would be an invented remedy.
filmability.human_consequence: NHTSA says entering a flooded roadway can cause loss of vehicle control, increasing the risk of a crash or injury. The April cars were unoccupied and no one was hurt. The consequence is conditional and must be shown as a risk, not as an event. Affected group: people who can now hail a ride in San Antonio, including airport travelers, and other road users who share a flooded road with one.
filmability.source_limit: Strongest limit: the record gives the mechanism in one sentence with no cause, speed, depth or narrative, and it gives no picture or video of the April event. The remedy is under development, and the interim 'weather-related constraints' are never defined. The October 14th post is silent on flooding. The company's September statements about flood-zone limits could not be read in an allowed source. The June pause reports conflict with the May reports, and dates are missing.
filmability.false_inference_to_prevent: A picture of a robotaxi in standing water implies several things the sources do not establish. (a) That any Waymo in any storm is in this condition today. (b) That the car in the picture is the April car, or a car in the recall. The recall covers 'certain' 5th and 6th generation systems, and a stock image may show neither. (c) That a rider was aboard, or was hurt. (d) That the fix has failed or is finished. Caption and source limit must say the recall covers potentially affected units, the April cars were empty and no injuries were reported, and the permanent remedy is pending.

must_not_say: Do not say the Waymo cars are unsafe, or that Waymo rides are safe now.
Do not name, imply or invent a rider or passenger in any event. The April cars were unoccupied, and TPR says no one was injured.
Do not say 3,791 or nearly 3,800 vehicles entered floodwater. Say potentially affected units under the recall.
Do not say the recall covers the entire fleet. NHTSA says certain 5th and 6th generation systems. (EVwire's 'entire fleet' is wrong.)
Do not say the recall remedy is finished, or that owners can schedule a free repair. The aggregator text conflicts with NHTSA.
Do not say the October 14th post addresses flooding or the recall. The fetched text does not.
Do not say October 14th was the airport's first day. Say airport trips opened to all app users on October 14th, after invited airport trips began March 31st.
Do not present 60 square miles as the current service area. It is the February limited area, per TPR.
Do not say the interim weather limits are in force today. The sources date the interim update to April 20th and do not confirm current status.

Do not state the cause of the April creek event beyond the recall text. Do not say a sensor failed, or that the maps caused it. The recall says the software may allow the behavior, and the interim update 'updated the vehicle maps'.
Do not give a speed or depth number. The 40 mph figure appears only in an unread PDF's search summary.
Do not say NHTSA demanded a remedy description or that a Part 573 was amended. Both come from unread or unverified summaries.
Do not say Waymo is, or is not, authorized by TxDMV. The TxDMV page does not show it.
Do not present the June pause reason (oncoming traffic, emergency vehicles) as fact. Sources conflict and the dates are missing.
Do not say the September 17th restart applies to everyone, or state the flood-zone limits as established fact. Those details come from an excluded source and an unread Axios body.
Do not quote Waymo's February safety multiples (ten-fold, 200 million miles). They were not verified verbatim.
Do not use 'drowned', 'sank', 'swept under' or 'crashed' for the April event. Use TPR's wording, 'swept up in flood waters and washed into Salado Creek'.
Do not give a single report date for the recall. Say May 2026 until the Part 573 PDF is read.
Do not say the recall was filed 'in April', and do not say Waymo was first to fix a flood issue.
Do not say the TxDMV power has been used against Waymo. No source shows that.

recommendation.verdict: Proceed to candidate, as an evidence-led news report. The angle is: anyone can hail a Waymo in San Antonio from October 14th, and the federal record still lists the flood fix as under development. Keep the film's one illustration disclosed and limited to the recall sentence.
conditions_before_spend: Re-fetch the TPR May 13th article and confirm the detection sentence (D5). If it fails, the opening falls back to the NHTSA mechanism sentence alone.
Extract and read the NHTSA Part 573 report and the May 11th acknowledgment letter inside the working tree (D7). Confirm the report date (D6) and the remedy status.
Read Waymo's own statement on the September changes, or the Axios body, before any claim about flood-zone limits or the restart (D11).
Resolve the pause reasons and dates (D10). Do not mention a pause beyond April to September until then.
Run dedupe.py check and place_photos.py for the airport and Salado Creek (D15).
Check the TxDMV Automated Motor Vehicle Lookup for Waymo's live authorization status before naming one (D14).
recommendation.fallback_if_conditions_fail: If the detection sentence and the interim measure cannot be confirmed, the film keeps only the two verified sentences (Waymo's October 14th opening and NHTSA's remedy status) plus the count card and the illustrated mechanism limited to 'may allow ... drive into standing water'. That is still a complete evidence-led film with an honest limit.
